subtopics.title: Dry corrosion and the oxide film
subtopics.theory_md:
**Dry (chemical) corrosion** is direct attack by dry gases ($\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$), mostly at high temperature, with no electrolyte. In **oxidation corrosion** the metal gives up electrons and the oxide forms on the surface: $\mathrm{2M \rightarrow 2M^{n+} + 2ne^-}$, $\mathrm{\tfrac{n}{2}O_2 + 2ne^- \rightarrow nO^{2-}}$. Later growth needs $\mathrm{M^{n+}}$ or $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ to diffuse through the film, so the **film decides the rate**:
- **Stable** (fine, adherent, non-porous): protective, Al, Cr, Sn, Pb, Cu.
- **Unstable**: oxide decomposes back to metal, Ag, Au, Pt.
- **Volatile**: oxide evaporates, $\mathrm{MoO_3}$.
- **Porous**: oxygen reaches the metal, Na, K, Mg, Ca.
subtopics.basics_md: Rust-proofing by nature: a metal wrapped in a tight, unbroken coat of its own oxide is sealed from air. If the coat is cracked, flaky or evaporates, the metal underneath keeps burning away.
key_points: Dry corrosion: gases, no electrolyte, usually high temperature
Oxidation: metal loses electrons, oxygen gains them, oxide film forms
Stable film protects; unstable film decomposes; volatile film evaporates; porous film lets oxygen through
Give an example metal for each film type

subtopics.title: Pilling-Bedworth rule
subtopics.theory_md:
$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{V_{oxide}}{V_{metal}} = \dfrac{M_{oxide}\,\rho_{metal}}{n\,M_{metal}\,\rho_{oxide}}$, where $n$ is the number of metal atoms in one oxide formula.
- **PBR < 1**: oxide cannot cover the metal, so it is porous and non-protective (Na 0.58, Mg 0.81).
- **PBR about 1 to 2**: compact, protective (Al 1.29).
- **PBR much greater than 2**: film is strained, cracks and flakes off, non-protective (W about 3.4).
subtopics.basics_md: Think of laying tiles on a floor. Too few tiles leave gaps (PBR < 1). Just enough covers it (1 to 2). Too many buckle and lift (> 2).
key_points: PBR = volume of oxide / volume of metal consumed
Below 1: porous, above about 2: cracks, between: protective
Formula with $n$, molar masses and densities
Examples Mg, Na (porous), Al (protective)

questions.q: Calculate the PBR of magnesium and predict whether MgO is protective. (Mg = 24.31 g/mol, $\rho$ = 1.74 g/cm$^3$; MgO = 40.30 g/mol, $\rho$ = 3.58 g/cm$^3$)
questions.model_answer_md:
$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{M_{oxide}\,\rho_{metal}}{n\,M_{metal}\,\rho_{oxide}}$, with $n = 1$ Mg atom per MgO.

$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{40.30 \times 1.74}{1 \times 24.31 \times 3.58} = \dfrac{70.12}{87.03} = 0.81$

Since 0.81 < 1, the oxide occupies less volume than the metal consumed, leaves gaps, is **porous and non-protective**.

questions.q: Calculate the PBR of aluminium. (Al = 26.98 g/mol, $\rho$ = 2.70 g/cm$^3$; $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ = 101.96 g/mol, $\rho$ = 3.95 g/cm$^3$)
questions.model_answer_md:
$n = 2$ Al atoms per $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$.

$\mathrm{PBR} = \dfrac{101.96 \times 2.70}{2 \times 26.98 \times 3.95} = \dfrac{275.3}{213.1} = 1.29$

1 < 1.29 < 2, so the film is compact and **protective**.

points: PBR = $V_{oxide}/V_{metal}$ with the molar-mass and density form
PBR about 1 to 2: compact, protective (Al, Cu)
Types of oxide layers cited (stable, unstable, volatile, porous)

subtopics.title: Wet corrosion: hydrogen evolution and oxygen absorption
subtopics.theory_md:
**Wet corrosion** needs a conducting liquid and a complete galvanic cell on the metal: **anode**, **cathode**, **electrolyte**, **metallic contact**.
- Anode: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$ (the metal dissolves).
- Cathode, **acidic, de-aerated**: **hydrogen evolution**, $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2\uparrow}$.
- Cathode, **neutral or alkaline, aerated**: **oxygen absorption**, $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Fe(OH)_2}$; with excess $\mathrm{O_2}$: $\mathrm{4Fe(OH)_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4Fe(OH)_3 \rightarrow Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (rust). Limited $\mathrm{O_2}$ gives black $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$.
Metal is lost at the **anode**; rust deposits near the **cathode**.
subtopics.basics_md: A tiny battery forms on the metal surface. One spot gives up electrons and dissolves; another spot receives them and reacts with acid or dissolved oxygen. Water is the wire between them.
key_points: Four conditions: anodic and cathodic areas, electrolyte, metallic contact, depolariser ($\mathrm{H^+}$ or $\mathrm{O_2}$)
Anode reaction is always oxidation of the metal
Hydrogen evolution in acid; oxygen absorption in neutral or alkaline aerated water

subtopics.title: Dry versus wet corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
Both mechanisms in one answer.
- **Dry (chemical)**: dry gases, **no electrolyte**, no separate anode and cathode, direct film formation, product at the site of attack, usually uniform; example: oxidation at high temperature.
- **Wet (electrochemical)**: needs a **conducting liquid**, many tiny galvanic cells, separate anode and cathode, metal lost at the anode and product near the cathode, often **localised**; example: rusting in moist air.
Dry corrosion is explained by the oxidation (film growth) mechanism; wet corrosion by the electrochemical theory.
subtopics.basics_md: Dry: the metal and gas react directly, like iron burning in hot air. Wet: water turns the surface into a battery.
key_points: Presence or absence of electrolyte is the main difference
Anode and cathode separate only in wet corrosion
Dry: uniform, product at site; wet: localised, product near cathode
Mechanism: oxidation versus electrochemical theory

subtopics.title: Galvanic corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
When **two different metals** are in electrical contact in an electrolyte, the **more active metal is the anode** and corrodes; the nobler one is the cathode and is protected. Driving force: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$. Zn-Cu: Zn dissolves, $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$, and in aerated water the Cu surface takes electrons, $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
The farther apart the two metals, the faster the anode corrodes. Rate $\propto$ cathode area / anode area, so a **small anode with a large cathode** is dangerous (steel rivet in a copper plate).
subtopics.basics_md: Put two unequal metals in salty water and join them: the keener one gives up electrons and wears away to protect the other.
key_points: Two dissimilar metals in contact with an electrolyte
More active metal is anode and corrodes
$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$
Small anode and large cathode is worst
Examples: Zn-Cu, steel bolt in copper sheet

subtopics.title: Concentration cell corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
On a **single metal**, parts in contact with electrolyte of different concentration or **aeration** form a cell.
- **Differential aeration** (most common): the **less aerated** part is the **anode** and corrodes; the well-aerated part is the cathode. Anode: $\mathrm{M \rightarrow M^{n+} + ne^-}$; cathode: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- **Metal-ion concentration**: the part in the **more dilute** solution of its ions is the anode. $E = \dfrac{0.0591}{n}\log\dfrac{C_2}{C_1}$ at 25 °C ($C_2 > C_1$).
Examples: waterline corrosion, pitting under dirt, crevice corrosion, pipe passing through clay (less aerated) and sand.
subtopics.basics_md: The same metal, but one patch is starved of oxygen. That patch pays the price and dissolves; the oxygen-rich patch is protected.
key_points: Single metal, different concentration or aeration
Less aerated part is anode
More dilute metal-ion part is anode
Nernst: $E = \frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_2}{C_1}$
Examples: waterline, pitting, crevice, buried pipe

subtopics.title: Passivity and corrosion resistance
subtopics.theory_md:
**Passivity** is the loss of chemical reactivity of a metal that is active in the electrochemical series, due to a very thin (about 0.0004 mm), **non-porous, adherent, self-healing** oxide film formed in an oxidising environment.
- Examples: Al ($\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$), Cr, Ti, Ni, stainless steel (at least 11 to 12% Cr), Fe in conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$.
- The film re-forms if scratched, in presence of oxygen.
- Passivity breaks down in $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ media or reducing conditions (pitting).
- Hence Al ($E^\circ = -1.66$ V) resists corrosion better than Fe ($-0.44$ V): Al forms protective $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ (PBR 1.29), Fe forms porous rust.
subtopics.basics_md: Position in the series says what a metal would like to do. A tight oxide skin decides what it can do.
key_points: Very thin, non-porous, adherent, self-healing oxide film
Oxidising environment needed
Examples: Al, Cr, Ti, stainless steel (Cr at least 11 to 12%)
Breaks down in chloride, giving pitting

subtopics.title: Iron in dilute and concentrated nitric acid
subtopics.theory_md:
**Dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$** acts as an acid and mild oxidant. Iron dissolves actively ($\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$) and the products are soluble, so no protective film forms: **rapid corrosion**.
**Concentrated $\mathrm{HNO_3}$** is a strong oxidising agent. It forms a very thin, compact, non-porous oxide film ($\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$/$\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$) on iron. Iron becomes **passive** and does not corrode further, nor does it displace Cu from $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ until the film is scratched.
Other passivating cases: Al, Cr in oxidising acids.
subtopics.basics_md: A strong oxidiser paints the metal with its own oxide in one stroke; a weak acid just eats the metal.

subtopics.title: Pitting corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
**Pitting** is localised attack producing small, **deep holes** while the rest of the surface is little affected.
- **Cause**: breakdown of the protective film (scratch, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, inclusions) or a deposit (sand, dust, drop) giving **differential aeration**.
- The spot under the deposit or film break is poorly aerated: **small anode**. The surroundings are the **large cathode**.
- Anode: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$; cathode: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- Small anode and large cathode make it intense and self-accelerating. Example: stainless steel in chloride solutions.
subtopics.basics_md: A small wound in the protective skin becomes a deep hole, because the wound and the healthy skin form their own battery.
key_points: Localised deep holes
Caused by film breakdown or deposit
Differential aeration: small anode, large cathode
Intense and self-accelerating
Example: stainless steel in chloride

subtopics.title: Soil corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
Soil acts as the electrolyte for buried pipes, cables and tank bottoms.
- **Factors**: moisture, aeration (a pipe through clay and sand corrodes in the clay by **differential aeration**), pH and salts, low resistivity, stray currents, and **sulphate-reducing bacteria** in waterlogged soil: $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-} + 8H^+ + 8e^- \rightarrow S^{2-} + 4H_2O}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + S^{2-} \rightarrow FeS}$ (black).
- **Prevention**: coatings (coal-tar, bitumen, epoxy, polyethylene wrap), cathodic protection (Mg/Zn anodes or impressed current), uniform backfill, drainage, insulation from stray currents.
subtopics.basics_md: Buried metal lies in a damp, uneven electrolyte. Wet clay and dry sand form cells; bacteria add more.

subtopics.title: Waterline, intergranular and stress corrosion
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Waterline corrosion**: in a partly filled tank, the metal just **below the waterline** (less oxygen) is the anode and corrodes; the part at the surface is the cathode.
- **Intergranular corrosion**: attack along grain boundaries. In austenitic stainless steel welded or heated at 500 to 800 °C, chromium carbide precipitates at boundaries, leaving Cr-depleted anodic zones (**weld decay**). Remedy: low-carbon grade, stabilise with Ti or Nb, or solution anneal.
- **Stress corrosion cracking**: tensile stress plus a specific environment. Examples: season cracking of brass in ammonia, caustic embrittlement of boiler steel with NaOH, stainless steel in chloride.
subtopics.basics_md: Three ways a normal metal is attacked unevenly: by the water level, by its own grain edges, and by stress with the wrong chemical.
key_points: Waterline: differential aeration just below water surface
Intergranular: grain boundary attacked, weld decay by Cr carbide
Stress corrosion: tensile stress plus specific environment

subtopics.title: Galvanic series and electrochemical series
subtopics.theory_md:
The **electrochemical series** ranks pure metals by standard electrode potential (1 M ions, 25 °C, hydrogen as reference); it is thermodynamic. The **galvanic series** ranks metals and alloys by their potential in an actual medium such as sea water; it tells which one corrodes in a real couple, includes alloys and passive states, and may differ in order.
- **Noble** metals (Ag, Cu, Au, Pt; positive $E^\circ$) are below hydrogen, do not displace $\mathrm{H_2}$, and form protective or unstable films.
- **Active** metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) corrode readily. In a couple the one higher in the series is the anode.
subtopics.basics_md: Textbook series: ideal lab conditions. Galvanic series: what really happens in sea water.
key_points: Electrochemical series: pure metals, standard conditions

subtopics.title: Predicting the corroding metal in a couple
subtopics.theory_md:
In a couple the metal with the lower (more negative) $E^\circ$ is the **anode**: $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$. The bigger the gap, the faster it corrodes.
$E^\circ$ (V): Mg $-2.37$, Al $-1.66$, Zn $-0.76$, Fe $-0.44$, Ni $-0.25$, Sn $-0.14$, Cu $+0.34$, Ag $+0.80$.
Zn with Fe, Ni, Sn, Cu gives EMF $0.32, 0.51, 0.62, 1.10$ V, so Zn corrodes **most with Cu**. Fe-Cu: $0.34-(-0.44)=0.78$ V.
subtopics.basics_md: Compare the neighbours: the further apart two metals sit, the harder the weaker one is pulled apart.

EMF = cathode minus anode
Larger EMF means faster anode corrosion

subtopics.title: Factors from the nature of the metal
subtopics.theory_md:
1. **Position in the galvanic series**: more active metal corrodes faster; bigger gap in a couple, faster attack.
2. **Relative areas**: rate $\propto A_{cathode}/A_{anode}$. Small anode and large cathode corrodes intensely.
3. **Purity**: impurities form local cells, so impure metal corrodes faster.
4. **Nature of oxide film**: protective, porous, volatile.
5. **Overvoltage**: high $\mathrm{H_2}$ overvoltage slows corrosion.
6. **Physical state**: stressed and fine-grained parts are anodic.
7. **Passivity**; solubility and volatility of products.

subtopics.title: Factors from the environment
subtopics.theory_md:
1. **Temperature**: raises reaction and diffusion rates.
2. **Humidity**: above **critical humidity** (about 60 to 80% for Fe) a moisture film forms and rusting speeds up.
3. **Atmospheric impurities**: $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, NaCl increase acidity and conductivity.
4. **Suspended particles**: hygroscopic or active particles absorb moisture and gases.
5. **pH**: below 4 hydrogen evolution; 4 to 10 depends on oxygen; above about 10 iron is passive.
6. **Oxygen concentration**, flow and conductivity of the medium.
Saline water rusts iron faster: NaCl raises conductivity and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ breaks passive films.
subtopics.basics_md: Water, salt, acid gases and heat all help the little batteries on the metal to work.

subtopics.title: Design and selection of material
subtopics.theory_md:
Corrosion needs anode, cathode, electrolyte and contact; design removes these.
- **Material**: noble or passive metals (stainless steel, Ti, Al); pure metals; avoid dissimilar metals far apart in the series, or insulate them; alloys for the medium (Cu-Ni for sea water).
- **Design**: keep the anode large and cathode small (copper plates with steel rivets are bad); insulating washers; avoid crevices, sharp corners, stagnant pockets; prefer welding to riveting; sloping drainable tank bottoms; uniform aeration; easy inspection and repainting.

subtopics.title: Sacrificial anodic protection
subtopics.theory_md:
The structure is connected by a wire to a **more active metal** (Mg, Zn, Al or alloys) that becomes the anode and corrodes ('sacrificed'); the structure becomes the cathode and is protected.
- Anode: $\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$; cathode (steel): $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$.
- Anodes are replaced periodically.
- Uses: buried pipelines and cables, ship hulls, tanks, boilers; Mg in water heaters.
- Merits: no power, simple, cheap; demerits: anode consumed, limited current.
Relative areas matter: a large cathode needs a good anode.
subtopics.basics_md: The sacrificial metal is the bodyguard who takes the hit.
key_points: Connect to more active metal: Mg, Zn, Al

subtopics.title: Impressed current cathodic protection and pipelines
subtopics.theory_md:
A DC source (rectifier) is connected with its **negative terminal to the structure** and the **positive terminal to an inert anode** (graphite, high-silicon iron, scrap iron, platinised Ti) buried in a backfill (coke breeze, gypsum, bentonite). Current flows through the soil to the pipe, forcing it to be the cathode.
| | Sacrificial | Impressed current |
|---|---|---|
| Power | not needed | needed |
| Cost | low initial | higher initial |
| Anode | consumed | inert, long life |
| Current | small fixed | large adjustable |
| Stray current | none | possible |
For an underground pipeline use Mg blocks in backfill (sacrificial) or a rectifier with graphite anodes (ICCP).

subtopics.title: Anodic and cathodic coatings
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Anodic coating**: coating metal is **more active** than the base (Zn, Al, Cd on iron). If scratched, the coating corrodes instead and the base is protected: $\mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$. Example: galvanised iron.
- **Cathodic coating**: coating metal is **nobler** than the base (Sn, Ni, Cr, Cu on iron). Protects only while intact; at a pore the base becomes a small anode and corrodes quickly. Example: tin plate.
Anodic coatings need not be pore-free; cathodic coatings must be.
subtopics.basics_md: Zinc coating guards iron even when broken. Tin coating only guards while perfect, and then makes things worse.
key_points: Anodic: coating more active (Zn on Fe)
Cathodic: coating nobler (Sn on Fe)
Anodic protects at scratches
Cathodic fails at pores, accelerates base corrosion

subtopics.title: Paint: ingredients and requisites
subtopics.theory_md:
A **paint** is a mechanical dispersion of **pigment** in a drying oil with thinner, drier, filler and plasticiser.
| Ingredient | Example | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Pigment | $\mathrm{TiO_2}$, red lead, ZnO | colour, opacity, UV protection |
| Vehicle | linseed oil | film-forming binder |
| Thinner | turpentine | lowers viscosity |
| Drier | Pb, Mn, Co linoleate | speeds drying |
| Extender | $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$, talc | cheaper, durable |
| Plasticiser | tricresyl phosphate | elasticity |
**Requisites**: tough adherent crack-free film, good spreading and hiding power, fast drying, glossy, resistant to weather and chemicals, stable colour.

subtopics.title: Pigment volume concentration and paint versus varnish
subtopics.theory_md:
**PVC** $= \dfrac{V_{pigment}}{V_{pigment}+V_{binder}} \times 100$ (dry film, thinner excluded). Below the critical PVC the binder wets all pigment: glossy, non-porous, durable film; above it, porous, matt, less protective.
**Paint vs varnish**: paint has pigment and is opaque; varnish is a resin solution with no pigment and is transparent. For **outdoor metals paint is better**: pigment screens UV, inhibitive pigments (red lead, zinc chromate) protect, thicker and more elastic film; varnish becomes brittle.
